glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The LORD answers Israel’s hungry complaints with quail and bread from heaven, and through the daily manna and the double portion before the Sabbath He teaches His people to trust Him one day at a time and to rest in His provision.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 16 takes place in the Wilderness of Sin, a month after Israel left Egypt and soon after the springs of Elim (15:27). Israel has not yet reached Sinai.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 16:1–3 — Israel Complains of Hunger in the Wilderness of Sin

  • Exodus 16:4–12 — The LORD Promises Bread from Heaven and Shows His Glory

  • Exodus 16:13–21 — Quail and Manna Are Given and Gathered Daily

  • Exodus 16:22–30 — The LORD Gives Israel the Sabbath Rest

  • Exodus 16:31–36 — Manna Is Kept Before the LORD for the Generations

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you. And the people shall go out and gather a certain quota every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in My law or not.” (Exodus 16:4)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
A month into the wilderness, hunger makes Egypt look good again. The people remember the “pots of meat” (16:3) and forget the whip. Moses tells them the truth about their grumbling: “Your complaints are not against us but against the LORD” (16:8). Yet the LORD answers before He rebukes. His glory appears in the cloud, and He promises meat at twilight and bread in the morning, “And you shall know that I am the LORD your God” (16:12).

The bread comes with a lesson built in. Each person gathers what he needs, and no one has too much or too little. On ordinary days, manna kept overnight breeds worms, so it must be gathered every morning, trusted rather than stored. On the sixth day the LORD commands them to gather twice as much and keep the extra overnight, and it does not spoil, because the seventh day is “a holy Sabbath to the LORD” (16:23). God teaches rest before He gives it as a commandment, and He makes rest possible by His own provision: “See! For the LORD has given you the Sabbath” (16:29). A jar of manna is kept before the LORD so later generations can see how He fed His people for forty years.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 16:1–3 — Israel Complains of Hunger in the Wilderness of Sin

In the Wilderness of Sin the whole congregation complains against Moses and Aaron. They wish they had died in Egypt beside the pots of meat instead of starving in the wilderness.

Exodus 16:4–12 — The LORD Promises Bread from Heaven and Shows His Glory

The LORD promises to rain bread from heaven, gathered daily as a test, with a double portion on the sixth day. Moses tells the people their complaints are against the LORD, the glory of the LORD appears in the cloud, and He promises meat and bread so they will know He is their God.

Exodus 16:13–21 — Quail and Manna Are Given and Gathered Daily

Quail cover the camp in the evening, and in the morning a fine flaky substance lies on the ground, the bread the LORD has given. Each gathers according to need, but on ordinary days manna kept until morning breeds worms and stinks.

Exodus 16:22–30 — The LORD Gives Israel the Sabbath Rest

On the sixth day the people gather twice as much, and Moses explains that tomorrow is a holy Sabbath to the LORD, and the stored manna does not spoil. When some go out on the seventh day and find nothing, the LORD rebukes them, and the people rest.

Exodus 16:31–36 — Manna Is Kept Before the LORD for the Generations

Israel calls the bread manna, and the LORD commands that a jar of it be kept for future generations to see. Aaron lays it up before the Testimony, and Israel eats manna for forty years, until they reach the border of Canaan.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 16 teaches dependence on God one day at a time. The manna could not be hoarded, so Israel had to trust that He would provide again tomorrow. Jesus takes up this chapter when He calls Himself “the bread of life” (John 6:35), the true bread from heaven that gives life to the world.

The chapter also shows that rest is God’s gift before it is His command. He gave a double portion so His people could stop working without fear. The Sabbath is woven into creation and into God’s provision, and believers are called to a deliberate weekly rhythm of ceasing and resting with the Lord.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Complaint and God’s patience. Israel grumbles against the LORD, and He answers by showing His glory and feeding them (16:2–3, 7–12).

Daily bread. On ordinary days the manna is gathered by need and cannot be kept overnight, while the sixth-day portion kept for the Sabbath does not spoil (16:4, 16–24).

Testing and obedience. The daily measure tests whether Israel will follow God’s instruction (16:4, 19–20, 27–28).

The gift of the Sabbath. God provides a double portion so His people can rest on the seventh day (16:22–30).

Remembering God’s provision. A jar of manna is kept before the LORD for future generations (16:32–35).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Wilderness of Sin (16:1). A desert region between Elim and Sinai. The name is a place name, unrelated to the English word “sin.”

Manna (16:31). The name Israel gave the bread from heaven. It looked like white coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey.

Omer (16:16, 36). A dry measure, one-tenth of an ephah, the daily portion for each person.

Sabbath (16:23). The seventh day, set apart as holy to the LORD for rest. Here Israel learns it through the manna, before the commandment at Sinai (20:8–11).

Before the Testimony (16:34). In front of the tablets of the covenant, later kept in the ark. The note looks ahead to the time after the tabernacle was built.

focus: Exodus 16 shows the LORD answering Israel’s hungry complaints in the Wilderness of Sin by giving quail and bread from heaven, and through that bread teaching His people to trust Him day by day. The chapter moves from complaint to promise, from daily gathering to the gift of the Sabbath, and finally to a jar of manna kept before the LORD as a testimony for later generations.

sections.title: Israel Complains of Hunger in the Wilderness of Sin
sections.summary: A month after leaving Egypt, the whole congregation reaches the Wilderness of Sin and complains against Moses and Aaron. They wish they had died in Egypt “when we sat by the pots of meat” (Exodus 16:3) rather than be brought out to die of hunger.

sections.title: The LORD Promises Bread from Heaven and Shows His Glory
sections.summary: The LORD promises, “I will rain bread from heaven for you” (Exodus 16:4), to be gathered daily as a test, with twice as much on the sixth day. Moses tells the people that their complaints are against the LORD, the glory of the LORD appears in the cloud, and the LORD promises meat at twilight and bread in the morning so that they will know that He is the LORD their God.

sections.title: Quail and Manna Are Given and Gathered Daily
sections.summary: Quail cover the camp in the evening, and in the morning a fine substance lies on the ground, which Moses calls “the bread which the LORD has given you to eat” (Exodus 16:15). Each gathers according to need, so that no one has too much or too little, but the manna some keep until morning breeds worms and stinks.

sections.title: The LORD Gives Israel the Sabbath Rest
sections.summary: On the sixth day the people gather twice as much, and Moses explains, “Tomorrow is a Sabbath rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD” (Exodus 16:23), and what is kept does not spoil. When some go out on the seventh day and find nothing, the LORD rebukes their refusal to keep His commands, and “the people rested on the seventh day” (Exodus 16:30).

sections.title: Manna Is Kept Before the LORD for the Generations
sections.summary: Israel names the bread manna, and Moses commands that an omer of it be kept so that later generations may see the bread the LORD gave in the wilderness. Aaron lays it up before the Testimony, and Israel eats manna forty years, until they come to the border of Canaan.

1.brief: The whole congregation journeys from Elim to the Wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai, a month after leaving Egypt. The next test comes as Israel moves deeper into the wilderness.
1.explain:
“And they journeyed from Elim, and all the congregation of the children of Israel came to the Wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai,”

Israel leaves the oasis of Elim and comes to “the Wilderness of Sin,” a desert region on the way to Mount Sinai.

“on the fifteenth day of the second month after they departed from the land of Egypt.”

The date is precise: “the fifteenth day of the second month,” one month after they left Egypt (12:6, 18; Numbers 33:3). Whatever food they brought from Egypt would likely be running low.
1.notes: The name Sin has nothing to do with the English word “sin.” It is probably related to the name Sinai. The region is usually placed in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, though its exact location is uncertain.

2.brief: The whole congregation complains against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The complaint now involves the entire people.
2.explain:
“Then the whole congregation of the children of Israel complained against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness.”

At Marah “the people” complained (15:24). Now it is “the whole congregation.” The grumbling has spread to the entire people, and it is aimed at both Moses and Aaron.

3.brief: The people wish they had died by the LORD’s hand in Egypt, “when we sat by the pots of meat,” and accuse Moses and Aaron of bringing them out to die of hunger. Hunger makes them remember Egypt as better than it was.
3.explain:
“And the children of Israel said to them, ‘Oh, that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt,”

The people wish they had died “by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt.” They mean they would rather have died with the Egyptians in the plagues than starve in the desert.

“when we sat by the pots of meat and when we ate bread to the full!”

Hunger makes them remember Egypt as a place of plenty. They recall “the pots of meat” and bread “to the full.” They forget the slavery, the beatings, and the murder of their sons. Hunger makes them remember Egypt as better than it was.

“For you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger.”

They accuse Moses and Aaron of bringing them out “to kill” them. Again they speak as though Moses, not God, brought them out (compare 14:11).

4.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “I will rain bread from heaven for you,” and the people are to gather a daily portion so that He may test whether they will walk in His law. God provides food in a way that teaches daily trust and obedience.
4.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you.”

God answers the complaint not with judgment but with provision. “I will rain bread from heaven.” The food will come down from above, as rain falls, and God Himself will give it.

“And the people shall go out and gather a certain quota every day,”

The bread will come “every day.” Each day the people must go out and gather “a certain quota,” a day’s portion. They cannot gather once and stock up.

“that I may test them, whether they will walk in My law or not.”

The daily gathering is a test. Will they “walk in My law,” following God’s instructions about how to gather? God provides food in a way that teaches daily trust and obedience.
4.notes: Moses later explains the lesson: God fed Israel with manna “that He might make you know that man shall not live by bread alone; but man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3). Jesus quotes these words when tempted in the wilderness (Matthew 4:4).

5.brief: On the sixth day they are to prepare what they bring in, and it will be twice as much as they gather on other days. The double portion looks ahead to the Sabbath rest God will teach them.
5.explain:
“And it shall be on the sixth day that they shall prepare what they bring in,”

On “the sixth day” something different will happen. The people are to “prepare” what they gather.

“and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.”

The sixth day will bring “twice as much.” God does not yet explain why. The double portion looks ahead to the Sabbath rest He will teach them (16:22–30).

6.brief: Moses and Aaron tell the people that at evening they will know that the LORD brought them out of Egypt. God’s provision will prove who rescued them.
6.explain:
“Then Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, ‘At evening you shall know that the LORD has brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

The people said Moses and Aaron brought them out to die (16:3). Moses and Aaron answer that by evening they will “know that the LORD has brought you out.” The coming meat will prove who rescued them.

7.brief: In the morning they will see “the glory of the LORD,” for He has heard their complaints against Him, and Moses and Aaron ask, “But what are we, that you complain against us?” The people’s grumbling is really directed at God.
7.explain:
“And in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD;”

In the morning they will “see the glory of the LORD.” This may refer to the manna, which reveals God’s glory in provision, or to the appearance of His glory in the cloud (16:10).

“for He hears your complaints against the LORD.”

The LORD “hears your complaints.” He hears them because, in the end, they are aimed at Him.

“But what are we, that you complain against us?”

Moses and Aaron say they are only God’s servants. “What are we?” Grumbling against them is really grumbling against the One who sent them.

8.brief: Moses says the LORD will give meat in the evening and bread in the morning, and adds, “Your complaints are not against us but against the LORD.” God hears and answers even complaints that were really against Him.
8.explain:
“Also Moses said, ‘This shall be seen when the LORD gives you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to the full;”

Moses spells out what will happen. God will give “meat” in the evening and “bread to the full” in the morning. The people complained that they once had meat and bread to the full (16:3). God will give them both.

“for the LORD hears your complaints which you make against Him.”

Moses repeats that God hears their complaints, and that the complaints are “against Him.”

“And what are we? Your complaints are not against us but against the LORD.”

Moses says it plainly: the people’s quarrel is with God. God hears and answers even complaints that were really against Him.

9.brief: Moses tells Aaron to call the congregation to “Come near before the LORD, for He has heard your complaints.” The people are summoned to stand before the God who has heard them.
9.explain:
“Then Moses spoke to Aaron, ‘Say to all the congregation of the children of Israel,”

Moses tells Aaron to speak to the whole congregation. Aaron serves as Moses’ spokesman, as God appointed (4:14–16).

“Come near before the LORD, for He has heard your complaints.”

The people are to “come near before the LORD.” They are summoned to stand before the God whose ears have heard every word they said.

10.brief: As Aaron speaks, the people look toward the wilderness, and “the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.” God reveals His glory to the complaining people before He feeds them.
10.explain:
“Now it came to pass, as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, that they looked toward the wilderness,”

As Aaron speaks, the people turn and look “toward the wilderness.”

“and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.”

The pillar of cloud that led them now shows God’s glory, perhaps as a brilliant light within it. God reveals His glory to the complaining people before He feeds them.

11.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses. God’s answer comes directly after His glory appears.
11.explain:
“And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,”

God speaks to Moses right after His glory appears. His answer comes from His presence.

12.brief: The LORD says He has heard Israel’s complaints and promises meat at twilight and bread in the morning, “And you shall know that I am the LORD your God.” The food will make God known to His people.
12.explain:
“I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel.”

God confirms what Moses said. “I have heard.” Nothing the people said escaped Him.

“Speak to them, saying, ‘At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread.”

God repeats the promise. Meat will come “at twilight,” and bread “in the morning.”

“And you shall know that I am the LORD your God.”

The purpose is that Israel will “know that I am the LORD your God.” The same purpose was given for the plagues, that Egypt would know the LORD (7:5; 14:4, 18). Now God will make Himself known to His own people through His care for them.

13.brief: Quail come up in the evening and cover the camp, and in the morning dew lies around the camp. God keeps His promise about the meat first.
13.explain:
“So it was that quails came up at evening and covered the camp,”

God keeps His promise that evening. “Quails came up” and “covered the camp.” Quail migrate across the Sinai region in spring and fall, and tired flocks often land on the ground where they can be caught by hand. God brought them at the very time He promised.

“and in the morning the dew lay all around the camp.”

In the morning, “the dew lay all around the camp.” The stage is set for the bread.
13.notes: Numbers 11:31–34 records a later gift of quail that came with judgment because of the people’s craving. Psalm 78:26–31 and Psalm 105:40 recall both events.

14.brief: When the dew lifts, a small round substance as fine as frost lies on the ground. The bread from heaven appears in a form Israel has never seen.
14.explain:
“And when the layer of dew lifted, there, on the surface of the wilderness, was a small round substance, as fine as frost on the ground.”

When the dew evaporates, something remains on the ground: “a small round substance, as fine as frost.” It is something Israel has never seen. The bread from heaven appears in a form they do not recognize.
14.notes:
Numbers 11:7–9 adds that the manna fell with the dew at night, was ground in mills or beaten in mortars, and was cooked in pans or made into cakes.

Some have connected the manna with natural substances found in Sinai, such as a sweet secretion left by insects on tamarisk trees. Such substances appear only in small amounts, at certain seasons, and do not match the daily supply, the double portion on the sixth day, or the absence on the Sabbath. The text presents the manna as God’s provision from heaven.

15.brief: The people ask one another, “What is it?” and Moses tells them, “This is the bread which the LORD has given you to eat.” The unfamiliar food is explained as God’s gift.
15.explain:
“So when the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, ‘What is it?’ For they did not know what it was.”

The people ask “What is it?” In Hebrew the question is man hu, which gives the food its name (16:31). The name itself records their surprise.

“And Moses said to them, ‘This is the bread which the LORD has given you to eat.”

Moses explains. The unfamiliar food is God’s gift, the bread He promised. The manna was real food for Israel’s bodies in the wilderness. Jesus later points to a greater gift: “Moses did not give you the bread from heaven, but My Father gives you the true bread from heaven,” and “I am the bread of life” (John 6:32, 35). He is the bread who gives eternal life (John 6:49–51).

16.brief: The LORD commands that each person gather an omer according to need, for everyone in his tent. God sets a measure that provides for every person.
16.explain:
“This is the thing which the LORD has commanded:”

God gives instructions for gathering.

“Let every man gather it according to each one’s need, one omer for each person, according to the number of persons;”

Each person is to gather “according to each one’s need.” The measure is “one omer for each person.” God sets a measure that provides for every person.

“let every man take for those who are in his tent.”

The head of each household gathers “for those who are in his tent,” the whole family.
16.notes: An omer is defined in 16:36 as one-tenth of an ephah. Estimates of its size vary, from about two to four quarts (two to four liters).

17.brief: The children of Israel gather, some more and some less. The people begin to gather in obedience, though in different amounts.
17.explain:
“Then the children of Israel did so and gathered, some more, some less.”

The people “gathered, some more, some less.” Some gathered more than an omer per person and some less, perhaps according to their strength or the size of their family.

18.brief: When they measure it, the one who gathered much has nothing left over and the one who gathered little has no lack, each having what he needs. God’s provision matches each person’s need.
18.explain:
“So when they measured it by omers, he who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack.”

When they measured, the result was the same for everyone. The one who gathered more “had nothing left over,” and the one who gathered less “had no lack.” God’s provision matched each person’s need.

“Every man had gathered according to each one’s need.”

Each household ended up with exactly what it needed. The verse does not explain how. Some think the people shared within families and the camp. Others see God’s hand making the measure come out right. Paul later quotes this verse when he urges the Corinthians to give generously to believers in need, using it to teach a fair sharing among God’s people (2 Corinthians 8:13–15).

19.brief: Moses says, “Let no one leave any of it till morning.” The daily portion is meant to be trusted, not stored.
19.explain:
“And Moses said, ‘Let no one leave any of it till morning.”

Moses tells them not to keep any “till morning.” They must trust that God will provide again the next day. The daily portion is meant to be trusted, not stored.

20.brief: Some do not heed Moses and keep part until morning, and it breeds worms and stinks, and Moses is angry with them. Hoarding God’s daily gift exposes a lack of trust.
20.explain:
“Notwithstanding they did not heed Moses.”

Some people “did not heed Moses.” They failed the test God set (16:4).

“But some of them left part of it until morning, and it bred worms and stank.”

The manna they kept “bred worms and stank.” Food kept against God’s word spoiled overnight. Hoarding God’s daily gift exposes a lack of trust.

“And Moses was angry with them.”

Moses is “angry” at their disobedience. God had given a clear command, and they ignored it.

21.brief: The people gather it every morning, each according to need, and when the sun grows hot it melts. The manna must be gathered daily and cannot be kept on ordinary days.
21.explain:
“So they gathered it every morning, every man according to his need.”

The pattern settles in. Every morning each person gathers “according to his need.”

“And when the sun became hot, it melted.”

When “the sun became hot,” the manna “melted.” It had to be gathered early. Like the spoiling overnight, the melting kept the people dependent on God day by day.

22.brief: On the sixth day the people gather twice as much, two omers each, and the rulers report this to Moses. The double portion comes just as God said in verse 5.
22.explain:
“And so it was, on the sixth day, that they gathered twice as much bread, two omers for each one.”

On “the sixth day” the people gathered “twice as much,” “two omers for each one.” This is what God had said would happen (16:5).

“And all the rulers of the congregation came and told Moses.”

The leaders notice and report to Moses. They do not yet understand the reason.

23.brief: Moses explains, “Tomorrow is a Sabbath rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD,” and tells them to prepare their food and keep the rest until morning. God’s provision teaches Israel the Sabbath before the law at Sinai.
23.explain:
“Then he said to them, ‘This is what the LORD has said:”

Moses explains with God’s word.

“Tomorrow is a Sabbath rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD.”

This is the first time the word “Sabbath” appears in Scripture. The day is “holy,” set apart “to the LORD.” God rested on the seventh day of creation (Genesis 2:2–3). Now He gives His people a day of rest.

“Bake what you will bake today, and boil what you will boil;”

The people are to cook what they need “today,” on the sixth day, so they need not work on the Sabbath.

“and lay up for yourselves all that remains, to be kept until morning.”

What is left over is to be kept “until morning.” On other days God forbade this (16:19). For the Sabbath He commands it. God’s provision teaches Israel the Sabbath before the law at Sinai.
23.notes: The Hebrew word Sabbath comes from a verb meaning to cease or to rest. The same root is used in Genesis 2:2–3, where God “rested” on the seventh day.

24.brief: The people lay it up till morning as Moses commanded, and it does not stink or breed worms. The same food that spoiled on other days keeps on the Sabbath because God provides for the rest He commands.
24.explain:
“So they laid it up till morning, as Moses commanded;”

This time the people obey. They keep the extra manna “as Moses commanded.”

“and it did not stink, nor were there any worms in it.”

The manna that spoiled on other nights stayed fresh. The same food that spoiled on other days keeps on the Sabbath because God provides for the rest He commands.

25.brief: Moses tells them to eat it that day, “for today is a Sabbath to the LORD,” and they will not find any in the field. The Sabbath is a day of rest made possible by God’s provision.
25.explain:
“Then Moses said, ‘Eat that today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD;”

Moses tells them to eat what they kept. The day belongs “to the LORD.”

“today you will not find it in the field.”

There will be no manna on the ground that day. The Sabbath is a day of rest made possible by God’s provision.

26.brief: “Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, there will be none.” The pattern of work and rest is built into God’s provision.
26.explain:
“Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, there will be none.”

Moses gives the pattern. Israel is to gather “six days,” and on “the seventh day” there will be “none.” Work and rest are built into God’s provision. The weekly rhythm comes before the command at Sinai (20:8–11).

27.brief: Some of the people go out to gather on the seventh day but find none. Their failure to trust God’s word leaves them empty-handed.
27.explain:
“Now it happened that some of the people went out on the seventh day to gather, but they found none.”

Some people went out anyway. They “found none.” They did not believe Moses’ word, and they came back empty-handed. Their failure to trust God’s word left them with nothing.

28.brief: The LORD asks Moses, “How long do you refuse to keep My commandments and My laws?” God rebukes the people’s disobedience.
28.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘How long do you refuse to keep My commandments and My laws?”

God rebukes the people. “How long do you refuse?” The same question God put to Pharaoh (10:3) He now puts to Israel. Though the words are spoken to Moses, the “you” is plural and addresses the whole people.

29.brief: “See! For the LORD has given you the Sabbath,” and gives bread for two days on the sixth day, so everyone is to stay in his place on the seventh. The Sabbath is God’s gift, and He provides what makes it possible.
29.explain:
“See! For the LORD has given you the Sabbath;”

God calls them to “See!” “The LORD has given you the Sabbath.” The Sabbath is God’s gift to His people.

“therefore He gives you on the sixth day bread for two days.”

The gift comes with provision. God gives “bread for two days” on the sixth day so they can rest on the seventh.

“Let every man remain in his place; let no man go out of his place on the seventh day.”

The people are to stay “in his place” and not go out to gather. The Sabbath is God’s gift, and He provides what makes it possible. This rest is given here, before the law at Sinai. Jesus, the Lord of the Sabbath, calls the weary to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28), and the rest believers begin to enjoy in His finished work looks toward unbroken communion with God (Hebrews 4:9–10). Believers are called to a serious, deliberate weekly rhythm of ceasing from ordinary work to be with Him, with liberty about which day they set apart (Romans 14:5–6).
29.notes: The Sabbath command was later given to Israel as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and His people (31:13–17).

30.brief: “So the people rested on the seventh day.” Israel learns to rest by trusting God’s provision.
30.explain:
“So the people rested on the seventh day.”

At last “the people rested.” Israel learns to rest by trusting God’s provision. They had been slaves, forced to work without rest. Now God gives them a day to cease.
30.notes: Deuteronomy 5:15 ties the Sabbath to Israel’s release from slavery: “remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there.”

31.brief: The house of Israel calls the bread Manna, and it is like white coriander seed and tastes like wafers made with honey. The name and description record the gift for later readers.
31.explain:
“And the house of Israel called its name Manna.”

The people name the bread “Manna,” from their question “What is it?” (16:15).

“And it was like white coriander seed, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.”

The narrator describes it. It looked “like white coriander seed,” small and round. It tasted “like wafers made with honey,” sweet. The name and description record the gift for later readers.
31.notes: Numbers 11:8 says it tasted like pastry prepared with oil. The difference may reflect how it was prepared.

32.brief: Moses relays the LORD’s command to keep an omer of manna for future generations, so they may see the bread God fed them in the wilderness. God wants His provision remembered.
32.explain:
“Then Moses said, ‘This is the thing which the LORD has commanded:”

Moses gives a further command from God.

“Fill an omer with it, to be kept for your generations,”

An “omer” of manna is to be kept “for your generations.” God wants a lasting memorial of His provision.

“that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

Future generations will “see the bread” with which God fed their ancestors. The jar of manna will be a testimony that God sustained His people. God wants His provision remembered.

33.brief: Moses tells Aaron to put an omer of manna in a pot and lay it up before the LORD for future generations. The memorial will be kept in God’s presence.
33.explain:
“And Moses said to Aaron, ‘Take a pot and put an omer of manna in it,”

Aaron is to put the manna in “a pot.” Hebrews 9:4 calls it “the golden pot that had the manna.”

“and lay it up before the LORD, to be kept for your generations.”

The pot is to be placed “before the LORD.” The memorial will be kept in God’s presence.
33.notes: Manna normally spoiled overnight (16:20). The preserved manna was itself a sign of God’s power, kept fresh for generations by His command.

34.brief: As the LORD commanded Moses, Aaron lays the manna up “before the Testimony,” to be kept. The narrator reports where Aaron placed it once the Testimony was in place, looking ahead to the time after the tabernacle was built.
34.explain:
“As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron laid it up before the Testimony, to be kept.”

Aaron obeyed and placed the manna “before the Testimony.” The Testimony refers to the tablets of the law kept in the ark (25:16, 21). The tabernacle and ark had not yet been made. The narrator reports where Aaron placed the manna once the Testimony was in place, looking ahead to the time after the tabernacle was built.

35.brief: The children of Israel eat manna forty years, until they come to the border of the land of Canaan. God’s daily provision continues through the whole wilderness journey.
35.explain:
“And the children of Israel ate manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land;”

The manna continued “forty years.” Every day of the wilderness journey, God fed His people.

“they ate manna until they came to the border of the land of Canaan.”

The manna stopped only when they reached the land. Joshua 5:12 records that it ceased the day after they ate the produce of Canaan. God’s daily provision continued through the whole wilderness journey.

36.brief: An omer is one-tenth of an ephah. The note explains the measure for later readers.
36.explain:
“Now an omer is one-tenth of an ephah.”

The narrator explains the measure for later readers. An “omer” is “one-tenth of an ephah.” The omer was a less familiar measure, so the note helps the reader understand the amount each person gathered.
36.notes: An ephah was a common dry measure, estimated at about half a bushel or a little more. The omer mentioned here is a different measure from the larger homer (Ezekiel 45:11).
